justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

The first entry belongs to the morning shift and records the indigo vat beside the west wall. The room thermometer showed sixty-eight degrees when Mara opened the door, and the water line was just below the brass mark. She checked the paper tag before touching the lid because the previous shift had moved the smaller test pot to the drying shelf. The tag said vat six, lot twenty-four B, and the cloth waiting on the cart was a roll of cotton twill weighing twelve kilos. The work order called for a deep blue finish for the Harbor Jacket run.

Section One: Morning Preparation
The recipe card was clipped to the left side of the rack, and its numbers matched the copy kept in the office binder. Mara measured four hundred grams of indigo paste and two hundred grams of reducing agent, then added both to the vat with the wooden paddle. She used the long paddle because the short one had a crack near its handle. The tap water ran cloudy for about ten seconds and then cleared, so she filled the marked pail to the line and poured it slowly. The log notes that the room fan was on low and the back window stayed shut while the mixture settled for twenty minutes.

At nine twelve, Jonah came in from the rinse room carrying the shade strip from Monday’s trial. He held it next to the sample card under the neutral lamp and said, “The blue is warmer than the sample we approved yesterday, but leave the second vat alone.” The first comparison was made before the strip had fully dried, so Mara waited while Jonah hung it on the cord by the sink. After another eight minutes, they checked again, and the difference looked smaller. “Uh-huh,” Mara said when Jonah asked whether she had written down the waiting time. She added the minutes beside the reading rather than on the back of the card.

The first skein went into the vat at nine forty-five and stayed submerged for six minutes. Mara turned it twice with the paddle and lifted it slowly so the liquid could drain back into the basin. The cloth looked almost black when wet and showed a green edge under the lamp. They hung it on the upper rail with a blank space between it and the older sample because the older sample had a faint rust stain near one corner. The wash water in the first bucket was pale blue, the second was nearly clear, and the third carried a few loose fibers from the raw edge.

Well, the second skein took the same six-minute dip, but Mara recorded a lower vat reading after checking the glass thermometer again. The figure was sixty-six degrees, and the room had cooled when the fan stopped by itself. She restarted it and told no one to add heat until the maintenance check was done. The switch plate had felt warm on Monday, and a small note about that was already pinned above the workbench. The recipe did not call for a temperature change, and she kept the original measure of paste and reducing agent for the next dip. The time and amount remained the same.

Section Two: Shade Checks
By eleven thirty, the first two skeins were dry enough to compare with the approved strip. Mara laid them on clean white paper and turned each one so the light fell across the twill in the same direction. The first was a shade lighter than the card at the folded edge, while the second matched the middle of the sample more closely. She wrote both observations without calling either one a pass. The foreman had asked for a record before lunch and had not asked for a decision. The card was returned to its sleeve, and the damp strips were moved to a separate rail.

Like the first pair, the next test pieces came from the same roll, but one had been cut near the selvedge and the other from the center. The selvedge piece took up color faster along one side and left a narrow pale line after rinsing. Mara noted the location and width in the margin, then checked the cloth ticket to confirm that the cut pieces came from lot twenty-four B. The ticket number matched the tag on the cart. She did not change the vat or add more paste. The remaining cloth was covered with a clean sheet and left on the cart until the afternoon operator arrived.

Actually, the scale reading for the unused reducing agent was different from the morning estimate because the first weigh had included the paper cup. Mara weighed the sealed container again and entered the net amount in the supply column. The difference was thirty grams, and she left the earlier figure visible with a note beside it so the next reader could see both readings. The container went back into the locked cabinet, and the cabinet key was returned to its hook. No material was taken from the reserve shelf. The office copy of the recipe still showed the same amounts as the card on the rack.

At the end of the shift, Mara recorded the rinse water temperature, the number of pieces tested, and the time the fan stopped. She left the three dry samples in labeled envelopes on the review table and kept the damp selvedge piece on the upper rail until it was fully dry. Jonah took the shade strip back to the office, but the approved card stayed in the binder beside the work order. The final note says that the second vat remained untouched and that the maintenance check was still pending. The north window was opened after the last rinse, and the room was left with the basin empty, the paddle rinsed, and the thermometer hanging beside the rack."}]
